summary: Specifies GIST, the General Internet Signalling Transport, which carries signalling messages along the path of a data flow. It is the base protocol of the Next Steps in Signalling (NSIS) framework and uses existing transport and security protocols. It is an Experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: A messenger who follows the same road as the package and delivers notes to every stop on the way.

questions: what is general internet signalling transport
what udp port does gist use
subtitle: A shared messenger layer that finds the next signalling node along a data flow's path and carries signalling messages to it.

tldr.problem: Applications that need to configure network devices along the path of a data flow, such as resource reservation or firewall control, all need the same plumbing: find the next signalling-capable node on the path and move messages to it reliably and securely.
tldr.mechanism: GIST discovers each adjacent peer with a Query, Response and Confirm handshake sent along the flow's path, then carries signalling messages hop by hop using UDP for small simple messages or TCP, optionally with TLS, for everything else.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5971 is an Experimental specification that provides the base protocol of the NSIS framework. Signalling applications plug in on top and GIST keeps their state out of its own business.

today: RFC 5971 is an Experimental specification, published in October 2010 for examination, experimental implementation and evaluation, and it is not on the Internet Standards Track. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What GIST Is For
sections.content:
Signalling means manipulating or monitoring state held in network elements. Examples named in the RFC are network resource reservation, firewall configuration and discovering path properties such as available bandwidth. Each such use is called a signalling application. This specification concentrates on path-coupled signalling, which controls resources on the nodes along the path taken by a particular data flow.

Every signalling application needs state management rules of its own, but the machinery for exchanging messages along the data path is largely shared. The NSIS framework (RFC 4080) splits the work into a common transport protocol and application-specific NSIS Signalling Layer Protocols (NSLPs). GIST, the General Internet Signalling Transport, is the concrete solution for the common part.

GIST deliberately does not handle signalling application state. It provides node discovery, message routing and message transport, and nothing else. It assumes other mechanisms control routing, so it complements protocols such as RSVP-TE and LDP rather than replacing them. It does not directly support multicast flows, and not every node on a path has to take part.
sections.eli5: GIST does the delivering and nothing else. The programs that use it decide what the notes say; GIST just finds the next stop and carries them there.

sections.title: Two Modes and Messaging Associations
sections.content:
GIST splits transport into a minimal part of its own and well-understood protocols for harder cases. It has two modes. Datagram mode (D-mode) is for small, infrequent messages with modest delay needs and no security requirements. A special case, Query mode (Q-mode), is used when no routing state exists. Connection mode (C-mode) is used for everything else: large messages, channel security and congestion control. This specification defines TCP as the initial C-mode transport and TLS as the initial channel security.

C-mode traffic runs over a messaging association (MA), a connection between two explicitly identified adjacent peers. An MA is bidirectional, is invisible to signalling applications, and is set up and torn down by GIST itself. There can be any number between two peers, though zero or one is the usual case. The two modes can be mixed along a path, for example D-mode at the edges and C-mode towards the core.

The signalling application never picks the mode. GIST decides from the message size and the transfer attributes the application states, such as whether delivery must be reliable or secured. When a message needs C-mode, GIST first runs the handshake in D-mode to identify the peer, then sets up the connection.

Transfer attributes are minimum requirements. GIST MAY deliver with stronger properties than requested, and a reliable message MUST be delivered exactly once or not at all, in order within a session.
sections.eli5: Small notes go as postcards, which are quick but can get lost. Big or secret notes go in a locked tube that GIST sets up first. The sender does not choose; GIST does.

sections.title: Routing Methods, Sessions and NSLP Identifiers
sections.content:
The details of finding the next peer depend on what is being signalled, so GIST packages them as a message routing method (MRM). Each MRM defines the message routing information (MRI) that describes where messages should go, how probe messages are encapsulated, what validity checks apply and how route changes are detected. This RFC defines two. The path-coupled MRM follows the route of an existing flow. The Loose-End MRM discovers GIST nodes with particular properties in the direction of a given address, for example a NAT along the upstream data path.

Every message belongs to a session, named by a 128-bit Session Identifier (SID) that is opaque to GIST. Routing state is indexed by the combination of MRI, SID and NSLPID. Including the SID matters for security: if state were keyed only by flow and application, an off-path attacker could simply claim to be the peer for a flow. Signalling applications MUST therefore choose SIDs that are cryptographically random.

Each NSLP is identified by a 16-bit NSLPID assigned by IANA. It is the only thing GIST knows about the signalling application. GIST keeps a routing state table with a validity timer per entry, usually one entry per direction (upstream and downstream), and purges entries that are not refreshed.
sections.eli5: Each note carries a secret session number and a label for which program it belongs to. GIST files its address book by flow, session and program, so nobody can easily trick it into sending notes to the wrong place.

sections.title: The Three-Way Handshake
sections.content:
Routing state is created by a handshake of three messages. The Querying node sends a Query along the flow's path, with a Router Alert Option so that GIST-aware routers notice it. Nodes that host the signalling application decide whether to peer; others forward the Query untouched. The node that decides to peer answers with a Response, and a Query always elicits one when the application agrees to peer. If a new messaging association is needed, it is set up right after the Query/Response exchange, always starting from the Querying node, and the Querying node then sends a Confirm over it.

The Query carries a Query-Cookie that the Response echoes, which lets the Querying node discard forged Responses. The Responding node MAY delay installing state until it gets a Confirm that echoes its Responder-Cookie. This is a return routability check, in the same spirit as the cookie exchange in SCTP, and it defends against attacks that resemble TCP SYN floods. The full handshake costs 1.5 round-trip times.

Routing state expires. A default lifetime of 30 seconds is RECOMMENDED, and the Querying node must refresh before then, between 1/2 and 3/4 of the way through the validity time, at a randomly chosen moment so that refreshes do not synchronise. There is no explicit teardown at the GIST level. An idle MA is kept for an MA-Hold-Time, also 30 seconds by default, and a peer that wants it kept alive sends an MA-Hello.

Peers that use channel security check the authenticated identity of the other side against an authorised peer database (APD). An unauthorised peer's association MUST be torn down. The RFC also describes multiplexing, where one association serves many flows between the same two nodes, matched by the Peer-Identity and Interface-Address in the Network-Layer-Information object.
sections.eli5: GIST shouts hello down the road. The first stop that cares shouts back. Then the first one says got it, and the two are friends. They repeat this now and then to check the road has not changed.

sections.title: Messages and the Common Header
sections.content:
GIST has six message types: Query, Response, Confirm, Data, Error and MA-Hello. Query, Response and Confirm form the handshake. Data simply carries an NSLP payload without changing GIST state. Error reports GIST-level problems and MA-Hello is a keepalive and diagnostic for associations. All signalling application data travels as an NSLP-Data payload inside these messages.

Every message starts with a fixed common header, followed by type-length-value objects in a fixed order for each message type. The header holds a version (this RFC defines version 1), a GIST hop count to stop looping, the message length in 32-bit words, the NSLPID and a message type. Four flags matter: C (the message must be interpretable without routing state), S (the IP source address is the signalling source address), R (a reply is requested) and E (explicitly routed, only for Data). The R flag MUST be set in every Query.

The objects include the MRI, the SID, the Network-Layer-Information (peer identity, interface address, routing state validity time and IP TTL), the cookies, a Stack-Proposal and Stack-Configuration-Data describing which protocol stacks can be used for an association, and the NSLP-Data. Each object has a 12-bit type and a 12-bit length in 32-bit words, plus two extensibility flags that say how unknown objects are treated.

The message type is a 7-bit field. IANA registered values 0 to 5 for the six types, with 56 to 63 for private or experimental use.
sections.eli5: Every GIST note starts with a small label saying what kind of note it is, how long it is, and which program it is for. After the label come the details, always in the same order.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Transport
sections.content:
D-mode messages travel in UDP. The UDP payload MUST begin with a 32-bit magic number, 0x4e04bda5, or the message is silently dropped. Normal encapsulation is used when the peer is already known: one UDP datagram addressed directly to the peer, with UDP checksums enabled. Q-mode encapsulation is used for Queries and when no routing state exists. The message is addressed to the flow's destination and carries a Router Alert Option so that GIST nodes along the way can intercept it. The destination UDP port is the well-known port 270, and the sender MUST set the Don't Fragment bit in IPv4.

Because Q-mode packets are intercepted by routers that were never addressed, they could disturb ordinary traffic. Two checks limit that. A node first filters on port 270 and then on the magic number. A packet that fails either check is forwarded as a normal IP datagram. GIST-unaware routers see only a normal packet.

Since D-mode has no built-in reliability, Queries are retransmitted with binary exponential backoff, starting from a timer T1 of 500 ms by default, up to a limit T2 that defaults to 64 times T1. Retransmitted Queries use different cookies. A single rate limiter covers all locally generated D-mode traffic, and a token bucket is RECOMMENDED with a mean rate of no more than 5 percent of the node's lowest-speed interface.

A message must go over C-mode if it needs reliable or secured delivery, or if its size plus a 64-byte allowance for IP and transport headers exceeds the limit. That limit is the path MTU if known, otherwise the smaller of the first-hop MTU and 576 bytes. The mandatory C-mode stack is TCP, and TLS over TCP is also required to be supported. TLS versions before 1.0 MUST NOT be negotiated, and TLS 1.2 is RECOMMENDED. For X.509 certificates the Querying node acts as the TLS client and the Responding node as the server.
sections.eli5: Notes that must find the right stop are stamped with a secret handshake word and sent to a special mailbox number, so only GIST stops pick them up. Everyone else just passes them along like normal mail.

sections.title: Route Changes and Local Repair
sections.content:
If IP routing changes, the peers GIST discovered may no longer be on the path. Because GIST re-runs its handshake periodically and signalling applications are expected to be soft-state, routes eventually repair themselves. If refresh times are long, the inconsistency could last a long time, so GIST adds prompt notification to signalling applications to allow local repair. GIST detects and records the change and informs the application. The application does the rest, since only it knows how to move its state.

A node can notice a route change in five ways: a local trigger from the forwarding table, an extended trigger from a link-state topology database, monitoring of C-mode packets for a different IP TTL or interface, data-plane monitoring by the signalling application, and the periodic Query/Response probing that every node MUST perform.

GIST classifies routing state as Good, Tentative or Bad. A Querying node can then verify the next hop from the forwarding table, enter Awaiting Refresh (still sending data), or enter Awaiting Response (which freezes signalling while state is repaired). For unstable routes or load balancing, GIST can hand the application an opaque SII-Handle for a previous peer, and Data messages sent that way carry the E flag and bypass the routing state tables.

The Querying side of each flow is modelled as a state machine with three states, Awaiting Response, Established and Awaiting Refresh. A top-level node machine and per-association machines complete the formal specification in the RFC.
sections.eli5: If the road changes, the messenger needs to notice. GIST watches for signs that the road moved, tells the program, and then goes back to find the new next stop.

sections.title: NATs, Tunnels and IPv4/IPv6
sections.content:
Signalling messages describe the flow in their payloads, so a NAT that rewrites packet headers without rewriting the payload would make the messages refer to the wrong flow. The base specification handles legacy NATs only by detecting them: when the IP source address does not match the interface address in the Network-Layer-Information, the handshake is ended, and an Object Type Error with the subcode Untranslated Object is returned where the MRI needs translation.

A more complete solution is a GIST-aware NAT. It rewrites the MRI and addressing objects in messages that carry the context-free flag (C=1) and inserts a NAT-Traversal object listing what it changed and keeping the original MRI. The details of NAT behaviour are informative here, and are left to a separate document.

For tunnels, a GIST packet is treated like any other packet and gets tunnel encapsulation, so it is not recognisable as GIST until it leaves the tunnel. Signalling for the tunnel itself is a separate session started by a tunnel endpoint. GIST is otherwise IP version neutral: Q-mode messages MUST use the IP version of the flow's MRI, and translators between IPv4 and IPv6 need to be GIST-aware.
sections.eli5: A NAT is like a mail room that rewrites the return address on envelopes. If GIST's note still mentions the old address inside, it gets confusing, so GIST either notices the problem or needs a mail room that knows how to fix the note too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC names three main concerns: protecting message content, keeping routing state intact so messages reach the right nodes, and preventing denial-of-service. Authorisation to perform signalling operations, such as allocating resources, is left to each signalling application. GIST has no authentication of its own and relies on the messaging association protocol, which for this version means TLS. TLS support is REQUIRED, but using it for any particular flow is OPTIONAL.

To protect routing state, an implementation can use ingress-filter style checks on the MRI, return routability through the Confirm, the authorised peer database, and SID segregation so that an attacker must guess the SID to overwrite existing state. Authentication shows who a node is, not that it is truly on the flow path.

Against denial-of-service, each Query produces at most one Response only slightly larger than itself, so GIST nodes cannot be used for amplification. Delayed state installation and cookies address SYN-flood-like state attacks. Cookies must be live, unpredictable and easy to validate, and the Responder-Cookie must be bound to the routing state it covers. Downgrade attacks on the protocol stack are countered because the Response does not depend on the Query's proposal and the Confirm echoes it, but that defence only works if the association has at least some integrity protection.

Residual threats remain. An on-path attacker that intercepts the initial Query can do most things to later signalling, and TLS with only a server certificate authenticates only one side. The RFC calls modes without mutual authentication at best transitional.
sections.eli5: GIST uses secret tokens so a stranger cannot pretend to be the next stop, and it makes sure answering a call never costs more than the call itself. But if a bad guy stands right on the road, GIST cannot fully stop them.

viz.caption: FIVE WAYS TO DETECT A ROUTE CHANGE

items.title: Local trigger
items.text: Forwarding table shows the next hop changed.

items.title: Extended trigger
items.text: Link-state topology database shows the path changed.

items.title: C-mode monitoring
items.text: C-mode packets arrive with a different TTL or interface.

items.title: Data plane monitoring
items.text: The signalling application notices the flow behaving differently.

items.title: GIST probing
items.text: Periodic Query/Response exchanges reveal changed information.

items.title: Filtering
items.text: Reject messages for flows that ingress filtering would rule out.

items.title: Return routability
items.text: Delay state until a Confirm echoes the Responder-Cookie.

items.title: Authorisation
items.text: Check the peer against the authorised peer database.

items.title: SID segregation
items.text: Include the SID in the routing state lookup.
